source: Hal R. Varian, Intermediate Microeconomics: A Modern Approach, 9th edition

entries.definition: The limit on affordable consumption bundles given prices and income.
entries.example: With $20, a buyer can afford two $6 meals and one $8 drink.

entries.definition: The value of the best alternative forgone when making a choice.
entries.example: Studying for an hour means giving up an hour of paid work.

entries.definition: A good whose price is normalized to one to express other prices relative to it.
entries.example: If bread is the numeraire, coffee costs three units of bread.

entries.definition: Bundles of goods that give a consumer the same satisfaction.
entries.example: A consumer is equally happy with two different combinations of tea and coffee.

entries.definition: The rate at which a consumer is willing to trade one good for another while maintaining utility.
entries.example: A buyer would give up two apples for one extra orange.

entries.definition: Goods a consumer is willing to exchange at a constant rate.
entries.example: Two brands of identical bottled water may be perfect substitutes.

entries.definition: Goods that are consumed together in fixed proportions.
entries.example: Left and right shoes are useful as pairs.

entries.definition: A numerical representation of a consumer's preferences.
entries.example: A utility function can rank baskets of food and clothing.

entries.definition: Preferences often represented by utility as a product of goods raised to powers.
entries.example: A household allocates spending between food and housing.

entries.definition: The most preferred affordable consumption bundle.
entries.example: A student chooses the best mix of books and meals within a budget.

entries.definition: A good whose demand rises as income increases, holding prices fixed.
entries.example: A consumer buys more restaurant meals after receiving a raise.

entries.definition: A good whose demand falls as income increases, holding prices fixed.
entries.example: A commuter switches from bus rides to taxis after income rises.

entries.definition: An inferior good whose quantity demanded rises when its own price rises.
entries.example: A severe budget squeeze may increase demand for a staple food.

entries.definition: Inferring preferences from observed choices under budget constraints.
entries.example: Choosing A when B was affordable reveals A is preferred to B.

entries.definition: A consistency condition ruling out certain reversals of revealed preference.
entries.example: If A is chosen over affordable B, B should not later be chosen over affordable A.

entries.definition: The demand change caused by a relative-price change while holding purchasing power appropriately adjusted.
entries.example: Cheaper tea encourages substitution away from coffee.

entries.definition: The demand change caused by a change in purchasing power after a price change.
entries.example: A fall in rice prices leaves more purchasing power for other goods.

entries.definition: A decomposition of the total price effect into substitution and income effects.
entries.example: A price cut changes demand through both substitution and purchasing power.

entries.definition: The initial bundle of goods or resources an agent owns.
entries.example: A farmer starts with 100 kilograms of wheat to sell or consume.

entries.definition: The value today of a future payment discounted at an interest rate.
entries.example: At 10% interest, $110 next year is worth $100 today.

entries.definition: Choosing consumption across different periods.
entries.example: A student saves some income now to spend after graduation.

entries.definition: Exploiting price differences for equivalent assets or payoffs.
entries.example: A trader buys an asset where it is cheaper and sells where it is dearer.

entries.definition: A sustained asset-price increase driven partly by expectations of further price rises.
entries.example: Investors buy an overpriced asset expecting to resell it later.

entries.definition: Probability-weighted utility across possible outcomes.
entries.example: A person compares a guaranteed payment with a risky lottery.

entries.definition: A preference for a certain payoff over a fair gamble with the same expected value.
entries.example: An investor prefers a guaranteed $100 to an equal-chance $0 or $200 gamble.

entries.definition: Reducing exposure to individual risks by spreading investments or activities.
entries.example: Holding shares in multiple industries reduces firm-specific risk.

entries.definition: A loss threshold associated with a specified probability and time horizon.
entries.example: A portfolio has a 5% chance of losing more than its daily VaR.

entries.definition: The difference between willingness to pay and the amount actually paid.
entries.example: A buyer willing to pay $30 pays $20 and gains $10 in surplus.

entries.definition: Revenue minus variable production costs in the standard short-run framework.
entries.example: A firm earns $500 in revenue with $300 in variable costs: surplus is $200.

entries.definition: The money needed after a price change to restore the original utility level.
entries.example: After rent rises, calculate compensation that restores the tenant's former welfare.

entries.definition: The sum of quantities demanded by individual consumers at each price.
entries.example: At $5, three customers demand 2, 3 and 4 units: market demand is 9.

entries.definition: The percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in price.
entries.example: A 10% price rise causing a 20% demand fall gives elasticity of -2.

entries.definition: The additional revenue from selling one more unit.
entries.example: A monopolist evaluates how selling another unit changes total revenue.

entries.definition: The percentage change in demand divided by the percentage change in income.
entries.example: If income rises 10% and demand rises 5%, income elasticity is 0.5.

entries.definition: A price and quantity at which quantity supplied equals quantity demanded.
entries.example: At $8, buyers and sellers both want to trade 100 units.

entries.definition: Comparing equilibria before and after an external change.
entries.example: Analyze the new equilibrium after a tax is introduced.

entries.definition: The reduction in total surplus caused by inefficient allocation.
entries.example: A tax prevents trades whose benefits exceed their costs.

entries.definition: The risk that an auction winner overestimates an item's value.
entries.example: The highest bidder overpays for an oil exploration license.

entries.definition: The additional output from one extra unit of input, holding other inputs fixed.
entries.example: An additional worker raises daily production from 40 to 46 units.

entries.definition: How output changes when all inputs change proportionally.
entries.example: Doubling labor and capital triples output: increasing returns to scale.

entries.definition: The rate of input substitution along an isoquant.
entries.example: A factory replaces some labor with machines while keeping output fixed.

entries.definition: Choosing feasible production decisions to maximize revenue minus economic costs.
entries.example: A firm expands output while marginal revenue exceeds marginal cost.

entries.definition: A past cost that cannot be recovered and should not affect marginal decisions.
entries.example: A nonrefundable software license is a sunk cost.

entries.definition: Choosing the least-cost input mix for a target output.
entries.example: A factory selects labor and machines to make 100 units at minimum cost.

entries.definition: The additional total cost of producing one more unit.
entries.example: Total cost rises from $90 to $97 when output rises by one: MC is $7.

entries.definition: Total cost divided by the quantity produced.
entries.example: Producing 50 units for $400 gives average cost of $8.

entries.definition: A market environment where individual firms take the market price as given.
entries.example: A small wheat farmer cannot influence the market price.

entries.definition: A short-run rule comparing price with avoidable operating costs.
entries.example: A firm shuts down temporarily if price is below minimum average variable cost.

entries.definition: Payment to a factor above the minimum needed to keep it in its current use.
entries.example: A scarce location earns rent due to its exceptional position.

entries.definition: Revenue exactly covers all economic costs including opportunity costs.
entries.example: At price equal to average cost, a competitive firm earns zero economic profit.

entries.definition: A market with a single seller of a product without close substitutes.
entries.example: An exclusive local utility may face no direct rival.

entries.definition: Setting price above marginal cost, with the markup related to demand elasticity.
entries.example: A monopolist with inelastic demand may charge a higher markup.

entries.definition: The price-cost margin divided by price, measuring monopoly markup.
entries.example: With price $10 and MC $6, the Lerner index is 0.4.

entries.definition: A market where one firm can serve demand at lower cost than multiple firms.
entries.example: A water-pipe network can have large fixed costs and scale economies.

entries.definition: Charging different prices for the same good not explained by cost differences.
entries.example: A cinema offers cheaper tickets to students than other adults.

entries.definition: Charging each customer their maximum willingness to pay for each unit.
entries.example: A seller perfectly tailors every price to each buyer's valuation.

entries.definition: Offering price schedules or product versions that induce self-selection.
entries.example: A utility charges different per-unit rates for different usage blocks.

entries.definition: Charging different observable customer groups different prices.
entries.example: A museum offers different admission prices for students and adults.

entries.definition: Selling multiple products together as a package.
entries.example: A software company sells a word processor and spreadsheet together.

entries.definition: A pricing scheme with a fixed entry fee and a per-unit charge.
entries.example: A gym charges a membership fee plus a fee per visit.

entries.definition: Competition among many sellers offering differentiated products.
entries.example: Coffee shops compete with distinct brands and locations.

entries.definition: Making products distinct in consumers' perceptions or characteristics.
entries.example: Two cafes differ in location, ambiance and service.

entries.definition: A market with a single buyer of an input or product.
entries.example: A remote town has only one major employer hiring local workers.

entries.definition: The extra total expenditure required to acquire one more unit of an input.
entries.example: A monopsonist may need to raise wages for existing workers to hire another.

entries.definition: The extra revenue generated by an additional unit of input.
entries.example: A worker adds 4 units sold for $5 each, generating $20 of revenue.

entries.definition: A market dominated by a small number of strategically interacting firms.
entries.example: Two major airlines compete on a particular route.

entries.definition: An equilibrium where firms choose quantities as best responses to rivals' quantities.
entries.example: Two producers simultaneously choose how many units to make.

entries.definition: A model in which firms strategically choose prices.
entries.example: Two sellers of identical goods compete by setting prices.

entries.definition: A sequential quantity game where a leader commits before a follower.
entries.example: One producer chooses output first and the rival responds.

entries.definition: Coordination among firms to raise joint profits by restricting competition.
entries.example: Rival producers agree to limit output and raise prices.

entries.definition: A table showing each player's payoff for combinations of strategies.
entries.example: A matrix displays profits when two firms choose high or low prices.

entries.definition: A strategy that yields a better payoff regardless of opponents' actions.
entries.example: A firm's low-price strategy beats its high-price strategy in every case.

entries.definition: A set of strategies where no player benefits from changing strategy alone.
entries.example: Neither of two firms can gain by changing its price unilaterally.

entries.definition: A game where individually attractive choices can produce a collectively worse result.
entries.example: Two firms cut prices even though both would gain from maintaining them.

entries.definition: A strategy that randomizes among available actions.
entries.example: A firm varies promotions unpredictably to avoid being anticipated.

entries.definition: A player's payoff-maximizing strategy given the other players' strategies.
entries.example: A firm chooses its best output after observing a rival's planned output.

entries.definition: An action that changes future incentives in a believable way.
entries.example: A company signs a costly long-term capacity contract before a rival enters.

entries.definition: The tendency to weigh losses more heavily than comparable gains.
entries.example: Losing $50 feels worse than gaining $50 feels good.

entries.definition: The influence of an initial reference number on later judgments.
entries.example: A high initial list price affects willingness to pay.

entries.definition: A diagram of feasible allocations of two goods between two agents.
entries.example: Two consumers trade apples and oranges within a fixed total supply.

entries.definition: An allocation where nobody can be made better off without making someone worse off.
entries.example: All mutually beneficial trades have been exhausted.
